passages.text: At dawn Peter came in and said, “Let Clement, his mother Mattidia, and my wife sit together in the carriage.” And so it was done. As we set out on the road toward Balaneae, my mother asked me how my father was doing. I said, “He went away in search of you and my twin brothers, Faustinus and Faustinianus, and cannot be found. I think he has died, given how long it has been, either suffering shipwreck, meeting disaster on the road, or wasting away with grief.” When she heard this, she became tearful and sighed in sorrow. Yet her joy at finding me somewhat softened the grief the recollection brought. We arrived at Balaneae. On the following day we came to Paltus, and from there to Gabala; on the next we arrived at Laodicea. There, before the gates, Nicetas and Aquila met us, kissed us warmly and led us to our lodging. Seeing that it was a fine, large city, Peter said, “It is worthwhile to stay here for some days, for generally a large population is better able to produce the people being sought.” Nicetas and Aquila asked me who this unfamiliar woman was. I said, “My mother, whom God granted me to recognize through my master Peter.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: given how long it has been
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase is read temporally, with a long interval understood from the father’s unresolved absence: that elapsed time grounds Clement’s inference of death. “Most likely” is a possible probability-oriented rendering, but it does not directly preserve the contextual basis in elapsed time; the revised main text therefore prefers the temporal interpretation. Death remains an inference expressed by “I think,” not verified knowledge.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the people being sought
lexical_decisions.rationale: Peter’s generalization about a crowd can refer to missing persons in this recognition narrative; it can also mean the people sought for his mission. The main text does not specify which group.

lexical_decisions.chosen: my master Peter
lexical_decisions.rationale: κύριος here is a respectful human title for Peter, not an identification with the divine Lord. “My lord Peter” is the more formal alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ καταφιλήσαντες ἦγον ἐπὶ τὴν ξενίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: kissed us warmly and led us to our lodging
lexical_decisions.rationale: καταφιλήσαντες expresses affectionate kissing; no separate embrace is added. The source elsewhere distinctly names embraces when it intends them.

passages.text: When she had had enough sleep and awakened, Peter began speaking with my mother about reverence for God, saying first, “Woman, I want you to know the way of life of our religion. We worship one God, who made the world you see, and we keep his law. Its first requirements include worshiping him alone, treating his name as holy, honoring parents, being chaste, and living pleasantly. In addition, since we do not live without distinctions, we do not partake of the nations’ table; indeed, we cannot even dine with them, because they live impurely. But whenever we persuade them to think and do what belongs to the truth, and baptize them with a certain thrice-blessed invocation, then we gather at table with them. Even if someone happens to be a father, mother, wife, child, brother, or anyone else who feels natural affection, we cannot dare to dine with that person: we do this as a distinctive religious practice. So do not regard your son’s not dining with you as an insult, until you think and do the same things as he does.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: living pleasantly
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied adjective’s adverbial form refers to pleasant living; it is not changed to a conjectural “uprightly” or made a command to indulgence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with a certain thrice-blessed invocation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular description of a naming or invocation is retained; no specific baptismal formula or persons are supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: we do this as a distinctive religious practice
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression can also be understood as “we do this especially on religious grounds.” The main wording keeps the religious distinction and does not present the rule as a universal modern obligation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ ἄλλος τις ἐκ φύσεως στοργὴν ἔχων
lexical_decisions.chosen: or anyone else who feels natural affection
lexical_decisions.rationale: The active participle ἔχων makes that other person the holder of affection. Its object is unexpressed and is not replaced by a different, unnamed person who feels affection toward this one.

passages.text: While my mother was saying this, the boys, who were listening as Peter had advised, could no longer contain themselves. They stood up and embraced her, weeping abundantly and covering her with kisses. She said, “What does this mean?” Peter answered, “Woman, steady your mind courageously, so that you may enjoy your children. These are your sons Faustinus and Faustinianus, whom you said had died in the depths. How they are alive, after dying in your presence on that extremely dreadful night, and how one of them is now called Nicetas and the other Aquila, they themselves will be able to tell you. We too have to learn it along with you.” When Peter said this, my mother was so overjoyed that she nearly died from faintness. When we revived her, she sat down, came to herself, and said, “My longed-for children, please tell us what happened to you after that terrible night.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: after dying in your presence
lexical_decisions.rationale: Peter echoes her belief about the shipwreck rather than independently asserting an actual death and resurrection. “Having died as far as you were concerned” is a contextual alternative; the main text keeps the sharper surviving wording.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on that extremely dreadful night
lexical_decisions.rationale: χαλεπωτάτῃ is superlative and may have elative force, “extremely dreadful.” This preserves its intensification while not requiring a uniquely worst night. “Most dreadful” is the formal superlative alternative; the later positive χαλεπή remains “terrible.”

passages.text: Nicetas, henceforth Faustinus, began to speak: “That very night, when the ship was breaking apart, as you know, some men who were not afraid to plunder in the depths picked us up and put us in a boat. Rowing, they took us sometimes along the shore and sometimes sent for provisions, bringing us to Strato’s Caesarea. There, with us weeping from hunger, fear, and blows—all to keep us from rashly saying anything they did not want said—and after also changing our names, they managed to sell us. A very distinguished woman named Justa, a convert to the Jews, bought us, kept us in the place of children, and diligently educated us in every branch of Greek learning. As we grew up and became sensible, we loved the religion and applied ourselves to learning, so that in discussions with the other nations we could expose their error. We also mastered the philosophers’ teachings, especially the most godless—I mean those of Epicurus and Pyrrho—so that we could refute them more effectively.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: kept us in the place of children
lexical_decisions.rationale: Their purchase and subsequent treatment are both retained. The text does not explicitly describe a legal adoption or manumission.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the most godless
lexical_decisions.rationale: The superlative belongs to the narrator’s evaluation of the philosophers, not an added evaluation by the translator.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κἀκεῖ δακρύοντας ἡμᾶς λιμῷ φόβῳ τε καὶ πληγαῖς, ὅπως μή τι προπετὲς λαλήσωμεν τῶν αὐτοῖς μὴ δοκούντων, ἔτι δὲ καὶ τὰ ὀνόματα ἡμῶν ἀλλάξαντες, πωλῆσαι ἠδυνήθησαν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: with us weeping from hunger, fear, and blows—all to keep us from rashly saying anything they did not want said—and after also changing our names, they managed to sell us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative hunger, fear, and blows accounts for the children’s weeping and coercive treatment, rather than directly describing the means of a sale. The ὅπως-clause gives the purpose of that coercion; the subsequent renaming is introduced as an additional act. The revision keeps those attachments instead of assigning the speech-prevention purpose exclusively to renaming.

passages.text: “Having become almost companions from childhood with a certain magician, Simon, we came close to being deceived through friendship. There is an account about a certain man: when he appears in kingship, the [ὁ ... ων] of those who have revered God will be able to live immortally and without pain. But these things, mother, will be explained to you more precisely at the proper time. Just when we were about to be deceived by Simon, a companion of our master Peter, called Zacchaeus, took us in and warned us not to be deceived by the magician. When Peter arrived, he brought us to him, so that, by giving us full assurance, he might persuade us about the matters pertaining to reverence for God. Therefore, mother, we also pray that you may share in the good things we have been granted, so that we may partake of salt and table together. This, then, mother, is why you thought we had died: on that dreadful night pirates carried us off on the open sea, while you supposed we had perished.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: in kingship
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase may indicate appearing in royal rule or within a kingdom; the main text chooses the former without supplying a realm or identifying the man.

lexical_decisions.chosen: salt and table
lexical_decisions.rationale: The concrete shared-meal language is retained rather than reduced to social friendship.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ φανέντος ἐν βασιλείᾳ τῶν θεοσεβησάντων ὁ ... ων ἀθανάτως καὶ ἀλύπως βιῶσαι ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: when he appears in kingship, the [ὁ ... ων] of those who have revered God will be able to live immortally and without pain
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text attaches τῶν θεοσεβησάντων, “of those who have revered God,” to the incomplete subject marked by ὁ ... ων. This is supported by the contrast between the appearing man and the group benefiting from immortal, painless life, but it does not restore that subject’s missing letters. A material alternative attaches the genitive to βασιλείᾳ: “when he appears in the kingdom/kingship of those who have revered God, the [ὁ ... ων] will be able to live immortally and without pain.” Neither attachment is uniquely established; the three-dot gap remains unchanged and no lost wording is supplied.

source_issues.issue: The edition prints a three-dot gap with surviving ὁ and ων around it. These are retained literally as [ὁ ... ων], without restoring a person, group, or participle. The surrounding phrase is therefore visibly incomplete; the missing content has not been recovered.

passages.text: After Faustinus said this, our mother fell at Peter’s feet, begging and requesting that he send for her hostess and baptize both her and the hostess immediately. “Let there be no day,” she said, “from the time I have recovered my own children, on which I am deprived of dining with them.” When we too joined our mother in pleading for this, Peter said, “What do you think? Am I alone unfeeling, because I do not want you to dine with your mother after I have baptized her today? But she must fast at least one day before being baptized. Even this is because she simply uttered a statement on her own behalf that I recognized as a sufficient expression of her faith; otherwise she needs many days to be weaned from Greek religion.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: she needs many days to be weaned from Greek religion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes being de-Hellenized, here in a discussion of religious preparation, not renouncing Greek language or ethnicity. “To be freed from pagan practice” is an alternative but less transparent about the Greek category.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after I have baptized her today
lexical_decisions.rationale: The nominative singular participle agrees with Peter, the speaker. The English explicitly makes him the baptizer, not the children. Its event is within the rhetorical question’s contemplated action, not a statement that baptism has already occurred.

source_issues.source_quote: ἀφ’ ἧς τὰ ἐμαυτῆς. ἀπέλαβον τέκνα
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a full stop after ἐμαυτῆς, interrupting the continuous grammatical connection with ἀπέλαβον τέκνα. The English reads the surviving words continuously as “from the time I have recovered my own children.” The supplied Greek and its printed punctuation are not changed; no missing wording is restored. This is a disclosed editorial punctuation feature, not an assertion of OCR error or publication-blocking source corruption.

passages.text: “Since your mother approaches baptism with faith, let her fast at least one day before baptism.” But she swore, “For two of the days that have passed, while telling the woman about the recognition, I was unable to partake of food because of my great joy, except for a little water yesterday alone.” Peter’s wife testified to her oath, saying, “She has indeed tasted nothing.” Aquila—or rather, henceforth Faustinianus—said, “Then nothing prevents her from being baptized.” Peter laughed and answered, “But this is not a baptismal fast, since it did not take place for that purpose.” Faustinus answered, “Perhaps, then, God, wishing our mother not to be separated from the table for even one day after recognizing us, arranged the fast beforehand. For just as she remained chaste in ignorance, doing what accords with the truth, so perhaps God has now arranged for her to fast a day beforehand, in ignorance, for the sake of the true baptism, so that from the very first day of recognizing us she may partake of salt with us.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: since it did not take place for that purpose
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied ἤ literally introduces “or.” The main English “since it did not take place for that purpose” treats this as an explanatory reformulation: the earlier abstention is not a baptismal fast precisely because it was not undertaken for baptism. A more source-transparent explanatory disjunction is “But this is not a baptismal fast—or, rather, it did not take place for that purpose.” This preserves the printed disjunctive form while making the reformulation readable. “Unless it took place for that purpose” is only a contextual paraphrase of the criterion, not a direct alternative rendering of the printed ἢ μὴ clause and not a different Greek reading. No source correction is asserted.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a day beforehand
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine day is understood from the surrounding fasting discussion; no longer duration is added.

passages.text: Peter said, “Let not evil overcome us by taking care and a mother’s affection as a pretext. Rather, let us—you, and I with you—hold out for today, and tomorrow she will be baptized. Indeed, the hour of today is not suitable for baptism.” And we all agreed together that it should be done this way.

lexical_decisions.chosen: evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: This can be abstract badness or personified evil. The main text leaves the personification without explicitly naming a devil.

lexical_decisions.chosen: let us—you, and I with you—hold out for today
lexical_decisions.rationale: The shared exhortation and repeated reference to “you” are both retained in grammatical English. The text calls for holding out through the day; no new independent baptismal requirement is supplied.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρόφασιν εὑροῦσα τὴν πρόνοιαν καὶ τεκούσης στοργήν
lexical_decisions.chosen: by taking care and a mother’s affection as a pretext
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόνοια can mean care, concern, or forethought, as well as providence. Its pairing here with a mother’s affection supports ordinary care as the excuse Peter warns against; the source does not name whose care it is. “By finding a pretext in providence and a mother’s affection” remains a lexical alternative, particularly in light of Faustinus’s preceding proposal of divine arrangement. The main text does not uniquely impose divine governance as the meaning.

passages.text: “But perhaps someone will say, ‘How many have perished because of chastity?’ I say it was because of insensibility. For a woman who becomes aware, or who finds that someone has become a suitor, must immediately flee association with him as she would a blazing fire or a rabid dog. This is what your mother did, truly loving the beauty of chastity. Therefore she was preserved and received with us the knowledge of the eternal kingdom. A woman who wants to remain chaste must know that, envied by evil, she has many who plot against her under the pretext of love. Yet by the single resolve to remain chaste, continuing honorable and gaining victory over them all, she will be able to be saved. For the prophet said that, even if someone does every good thing, for the single sin of committing adultery one must be punished.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν αἰσθανομένην ἢ γενομένου τινὸς ἐραστοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: a woman who becomes aware, or who finds that someone has become a suitor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text carries the perception expressed by αἰσθανομένην into the second alternative by ellipsis: “who finds” is not a second printed perception verb. γενομένου τινὸς ἐραστοῦ is a genitive absolute stating someone’s becoming a suitor. A viable alternative retains it as a circumstance of the required flight: “For the woman who becomes aware—or when someone has become a suitor—must immediately flee association with him.” The main text instead treats both alternatives as ways the danger becomes apparent, supported by the initial perception language and immediate call to flee. The printed ἤ is retained in both analyses. A smoother “who notices that someone has become a lover” suppresses that disjunction and is therefore only a paraphrase, not a direct rendering of this edition. ἐραστής can mean pursuing lover or suitor, not necessarily someone whose advances have been accepted.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: The agent can be personified evil or human wickedness; no particular demon or person is supplied.

passages.text: As Peter was saying this, he saw the good and chaste Mattidia weeping for joy. Thinking that she had become sorrowful at the recollection of what had happened, he said, “Take courage, woman. While many have suffered many evils because of adultery, you have not suffered because of chastity, and for this reason you did not die. And even if you had died, you would have had your soul saved. Did you leave your homeland, Rome, because of chastity? Yet through that occasion you found truth, the diadem of the everlasting kingdom. Have you been in danger in the depths? Yet you did not die, and if you had died, the depths themselves would have become baptism for you, dying for chastity, toward your soul’s salvation. Were you separated from your children? For a little while: coming from legitimate seed, they have been found in better circumstances. Did you beg for food while starving? Yet you did not defile your body through prostitution. Did you torment your body? Yet you saved your soul. Did you flee an adulterer so as not to defile your husband’s bed? Yet, because of chastity, God, who knows of your flight, will fill the husband’s place. Were you grieved and left alone, separated for a little while from husband and children? Yet you were bound to leave them all at death’s appointed time. Better that you were separated willingly because of chastity than that, later, unwillingly, you should perish in those very sins.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: you have not suffered because of chastity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negative is retained, though the surrounding account relates her hardships to protecting chastity. It can contrast the true cause of suffering with its occasion, but the translation does not rewrite it as “you suffered because of chastity.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτός σοι ὁ βυθὸς διὰ σωφροσύνην θνησκούσῃ βάπτισμα ἐγίνετο
lexical_decisions.chosen: the depths themselves would have become baptism for you, dying for chastity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The conditional claim of baptism through death for chastity is explicitly the speaker’s; no sacramental qualification is inserted to reconcile it with the following teaching.

lexical_decisions.chosen: coming from legitimate seed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The language concerns the children’s origin from a legitimate union. The main text retains seed imagery and does not add a biological or doctrinal theory.

lexical_decisions.chosen: will fill the husband’s place
lexical_decisions.rationale: The promised replacement or fulfillment of the husband’s place is retained; its precise nature is not defined as sexual or institutional.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἅτινα γνησίας ἰόντα σπορᾶς ἐν τοῖς κρείττοσιν εὕρηται.
lexical_decisions.chosen: coming from legitimate seed, they have been found in better circumstances
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes τοῖς κρείττοσιν as neuter, referring to better circumstances, supported by the recovery of the children after danger and separation. “Among better things” is a more literal neuter rendering but can obscure the situational sense. The same form permits a masculine interpretation, “among better people,” which would locate them with a better group, for example their present associates, rather than characterize their circumstances. Neither interpretation is uniquely established; the legitimate-origin wording is retained separately and no particular group is named.
